title: Define an algorithm. Write any four characteristics of a good algorithm.
chunks: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics: Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps. Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined. Input: Has zero or more inputs. Output: Produces one or more outputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time.

title: What is pseudocode? Mention two advantages of representing an algorithm using pseudocode.
chunks: Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages: Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code. Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile.

title: Differentiate between time complexity and space complexity with one example.
chunks: Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input. Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1).

title: Define Big-O notation.
chunks: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity.

title: What is the difference between best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis?
chunks: Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n. Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound). Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n.

title: What is asymptotic analysis? Why is it preferred over measuring execution time?
chunks: Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency.

title: What is amortized analysis? Explain the aggregate method in one or two sentences.
chunks: Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive. Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n .

title: Find the time complexity of the following code: sum = 0; a = 5; b = 10; sum = a + b; printf("%d", sum);
chunks: The time complexity is O(1) (constant time) because there are no loops or recursion. The number of basic operations (assignments, addition, printing) is fixed and independent of any input size.

title: Find the time complexity of the following code: if (n > 100) x = x + 1; else x = x - 1; Also mention the best and worst case.
chunks: The time complexity is O(1) . The condition evaluation takes O(1) time, and both the if block and else block contain basic arithmetic operations taking O(1) time. Best case: O(1) Worst case: O(1)

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { printf("%d", i); }
chunks: The loop variable i goes from 1 to n , incrementing by 1 each time. The loop runs exactly n times. Number of iterations: n . Final time complexity: O(n) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 2) { count++; }
chunks: The loop variable i starts at 1 and increases by 2 in each iteration (1, 3, 5, ..., n). The loop runs roughly n/2 times. Execution count: n/2 times. Final time complexity: O(n) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } }
chunks: The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n 2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } }
chunks: The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop runs i times. The total number of executions is the sum of the first n integers: Summation: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = (n 2 + n)/2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i * 2) { printf("%d", i); }
chunks: The loop variable i starts at 1 and multiplies by 2 each time. Sequence of i values: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2 k . The loop terminates when 2 k > n, which means k ≈ log 2 (n). The total iterations is roughly log 2 (n). Final time complexity: O(log n) .

title: Define algorithm correctness. Differentiate between partial correctness and total correctness with suitable examples.
chunks: Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications. Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false.

title: What is a loop invariant? Explain the three steps—initialization, maintenance, and termination—used to prove the correctness of an algorithm.
chunks: A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct.

title: Explain how loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm.
chunks: In sorting algorithms like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i , the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.' Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: During iteration i , the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted. Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness.

title: Explain the difference between BUILD-MAX-HEAP and MAX-HEAPIFY.
chunks: MAX-HEAPIFY: Maintains the max-heap property for a given node, assuming its left and right subtrees are already max heaps. It has a time complexity of O(log n). BUILD-MAX-HEAP: Constructs a max heap from an unordered array by calling MAX-HEAPIFY in a bottom-up manner on all non-leaf nodes. It has a time complexity of O(n).

title: Define a heap. Differentiate between a Max Heap and a Min Heap.
chunks: A Heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap property, typically implemented as an almost complete binary tree. Max Heap: The value of each node is greater than or equal to the values of its children. The largest element is at the root. Example: [100, 19, 36] Min Heap: The value of each node is less than or equal to the values of its children. The smallest element is at the root. Example: [1, 2, 3]

title: Define the Divide and Conquer paradigm. Explain its three basic steps with a suitable example.
chunks: Divide and Conquer Paradigm The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem. It consists of three basic steps: Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems. Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case). Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem. Example: Merge Sort In Merge Sort: Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2 . Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort. Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array.

title: What are the divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm?
chunks: The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are: Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem. Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division. Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem.

title: Explain the general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm. How is it different from an iterative algorithm?
chunks: General Structure The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively: Algorithm DAndC(P) { if Small(P) then return S(P); // Solve directly else { Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1; Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems; return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk)); } } Difference from Iterative Algorithms Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks. State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters). Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large).

title: Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique. Give reasons for your answer: Binary Search, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Bubble Sort
chunks: Binary Search: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index). Merge Sort: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine). Quick Sort: Yes . It chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place. Bubble Sort: No . It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion.

title: Explain the advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach.
chunks: Advantages Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems. Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors. Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache. Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting. Limitations Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches. Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space. Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming).

title: What is a recurrence relation? Explain its role in analyzing the time complexity of recursive algorithms.
chunks: A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs. Role in Analyzing Time Complexity: When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2 , and merging takes linear time O(n) . This gives the recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)).

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0. Proof by induction: Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2). Substitute this into the recurrence: T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if: c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n -c · n + n ≤ 0 c ≥ 1 Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(n log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 Guess: T(n) = O(log n). We prove T(n) ≤ c · log n for some constant c. Proof by induction: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c · log(n/2) Substitute into recurrence: T(n) ≤ c · log(n/2) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · (log n - 1) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · log n - c + 1 We want T(n) ≤ c · log n. This requires: - c + 1 ≤ 0 ⇒ c ≥ 1 Since we can find a constant c (c ≥ 1) such that the condition holds, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
chunks: The Master Theorem applies to recurrences of the form: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) Given: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n a = 2 b = 2 f(n) = n Calculate n log b a : n log 2 2 = n 1 = n Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = n, and n log b a = n. They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log b a log n) Result: T(n) = Θ(n log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n
chunks: Given: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n a = 4 b = 2 f(n) = n Calculate n log b a : n log 2 4 = n 2 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = O(n 2 - ε ) for ε = 1. Since f(n) grows polynomially slower than n log b a , this is Case 1 of the Master Theorem. Formula for Case 1: T(n) = Θ(n log b a ) Result: T(n) = Θ(n 2 )

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n²
chunks: Given: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² a = 4 b = 2 f(n) = n² Calculate n log b a : n log 2 4 = n 2 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = n² and n log b a = n². They are equal. This matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log b a log n) Result: T(n) = Θ(n² log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n²
chunks: Given: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² a = 8 b = 2 f(n) = n² Calculate n log b a : n log 2 8 = n 3 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = O(n 3 - ε ) for ε = 1. Since f(n) grows polynomially slower than n log b a , this is Case 1 of the Master Theorem. Formula for Case 1: T(n) = Θ(n log b a ) Result: T(n) = Θ(n 3 )

title: Solve the following recurrence using the Master Method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
chunks: Given: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 a = 1 b = 2 f(n) = 1 (which is n 0 ) Calculate n log b a : n log 2 1 = n 0 = 1 Compare f(n) with n log b a : f(n) = 1, and n log b a = 1. They are equal, which matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem (f(n) = Θ(n log b a )). Formula for Case 2: T(n) = Θ(n log b a log n) Result: T(n) = Θ(1 · log n) = Θ(log n)

title: Explain why Binary Search requires the input array to be sorted. What happens if Binary Search is applied to an unsorted array?
chunks: Why Sorting is Required: Binary search fundamentally relies on the ordering of elements. It compares the target value to the middle element and mathematically eliminates half of the remaining search space based on that comparison. If target < mid , it knows the target must be in the left half, because all elements in the left half are smaller than the middle element. If Applied to an Unsorted Array: The logic breaks down. Comparing the target to the middle element gives no reliable information about where the target might be located in the rest of the array. The search might discard the half that actually contains the target, leading to a false negative (returning "not found" even when the element exists).

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array.
chunks: The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves. Divide: Split the array into two halves. Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half. Base Cases: If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min. If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min. Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min.

title: Explain the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort.
chunks: Best Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Average Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function. Worst Case: O(n²) Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)

title: Compare conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication with respect to the number of multiplications and asymptotic time complexity.
chunks: Feature Conventional Matrix Multiplication Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices. Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically). Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead). Recurrence Relation T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) Asymptotic Time Complexity O(n 3 ) O(n log 2 7 ) ≈ O(n 2.81 ) Conclusion: Strassen's algorithm reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, bringing down the asymptotic time complexity. However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices.

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers.
chunks: When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up. Process: Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts). Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²). Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively: P1 = A * C P2 = B * D P3 = (A + B) * (C + D) The middle term (AD + BC) is derived as P3 - P1 - P2 . Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) , improving the time complexity to O(n log 2 3 ) ≈ O(n 1.585 ).

title: Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm? Explain.
chunks: Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm. Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved.

title: When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort?
chunks: Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios: Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not. Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice). Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists. External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.

Unit I: Introduction & Foundations CO1

Algorithm Fundamentals A rigorous sequence of unambiguous computational steps transforming input to output. Crucial properties include definiteness (unambiguous steps) and effectiveness (basic feasible operations). Example: Euclid's algorithm for GCD(a,b) where a=12, b=8 yields 4 via systematic reduction.

Loop Invariants (Correctness Proofs) Formal logical assertions that remain true before, during, and after loop execution, utilized inductively to prove algorithmic correctness. Example: In Insertion Sort, `A[1...i-1]` is always sorted before the i-th iteration commences. Pro Tip: Examiners test initialization, maintenance, and termination. Ensure the termination property directly implies the overall postcondition.

Asymptotic Notations Mathematical abstractions characterizing growth rates: O(n) (asymptotic upper bound, worst-case), Ω(n) (lower bound, best-case), and Θ(n) (tight bound, average-case). Example: Mergesort is strictly Θ(n log n) as best and worst-case trees have identical depth.

Recurrence Solving (Substitution) A deductive technique establishing asymptotic complexity by positing a bound and applying mathematical induction to verify it against the recurrence relation. Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. Guess O(n log n), prove T(n) ≤ c(n log n) inductively. Exam Trap: When using Substitution, you must explicitly prove the exact form of your guess. Do not ignore lower-order terms during the inductive step!

How to Analyze Time Complexity Method Step 1: Identify the basic operation (comparison, assignment, arithmetic). Step 2: Count how many times it executes as a function of input size n . Loop Pattern Complexity Reasoning for i = 1 to n O(n) Linear iteration Nested: for i…n → for j…n O(n²) n × n iterations Nested: for i…n → for j…i O(n²) Sum 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2 for i = 1; i ≤ n; i = i*2 O(log n) Halving pattern: runs log₂n times Linear outer × log inner O(n log n) n × log n Big-O (O): Upper bound (worst case). Big-Ω: Lower bound (best case). Big-Θ: Tight bound (both).
Unit II: Core Algorithmic Paradigms CO2

Divide and Conquer Methodology A paradigm that recursively partitions a problem into disjoint subproblems, solves them, and amalgamates their solutions. Relies heavily on recurrence relations. Example: Strassen's Matrix Multiplication reduces subproblems from 8 to 7, dropping complexity to O(n^2.81).

Master Theorem Deep-Dive A deterministic method for solving recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Compares f(n) against n^(log_b(a)) using polynomial boundedness. Example: T(n) = 9T(n/3) + n. a=9, b=3, log_3(9)=2. n^2 > n, hence Case 1: T(n) = Θ(n^2). Exam Trap: The Master Theorem ONLY applies if the difference between f(n) and n^(log_b(a)) is polynomially large. It fails for T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n!

Greedy Paradigm & Matroids An optimization strategy making locally optimal choices with the heuristic that it converges to a global optimum. Only valid if the problem exhibits the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Example: Huffman Coding optimally minimizes prefix-free code length by greedily merging lowest frequency nodes.

Paradigm Decision Tree flowchart TD A[Optimization Problem] --> B{Overlapping Subproblems?} B -- Yes --> C(Dynamic Programming) B -- No --> D{Optimal Substructure?} D -- Yes & Greedy Choice --> E(Greedy Algorithm) D -- Yes & Disjoint --> F(Divide & Conquer) Example: Use this mental model to quickly classify DP (Fibonacci) vs Divide & Conquer (Merge Sort).

Bubble Sort Method Idea: Repeatedly swap adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest unsorted element "bubbles" to its correct position at the end. Steps: For each pass (i = 0 to n-2): compare arr[j] with arr[j+1] for j = 0 to n-i-2. Swap if arr[j] > arr[j+1]. Stop early if no swaps in a pass (optimized). Complexity: Best O(n) [already sorted, optimized], Worst/Avg O(n²). Stable: Yes. In-place: Yes.

Selection Sort Method Idea: Find the minimum element from the unsorted part and place it at the beginning. Steps: For i = 0 to n-2: scan arr[i+1…n-1] to find the minimum. Swap it with arr[i]. Complexity: Best/Worst/Avg O(n²) — always scans the full remaining array. Stable: No (swaps may break order). In-place: Yes.

Insertion Sort Method Idea: Build a sorted subarray one element at a time by inserting each new element into its correct position. Steps: For i = 1 to n-1: take key = arr[i]. Shift all elements in arr[0…i-1] that are greater than key one position right. Insert key at the gap. Complexity: Best O(n) [already sorted], Worst/Avg O(n²). Stable: Yes. In-place: Yes. Best for small or nearly-sorted arrays.

Heap Sort Method Idea: Build a Max Heap from the array, then repeatedly extract the maximum (root) and place it at the end. Steps: (1) Build Max Heap using bottom-up heapify: start from last non-leaf node (index n/2 - 1) down to 0, calling heapify on each. (2) For i = n-1 down to 1: swap root (max) with arr[i], reduce heap size, heapify root. Complexity: Best/Worst/Avg O(n log n). Stable: No. In-place: Yes.

Counting Sort Method Idea: Count occurrences of each value, then compute cumulative counts to place each element directly into its sorted position. Steps: (1) Find max value k. (2) Create count array C[0…k], count occurrences. (3) Compute prefix sums: C[i] += C[i-1]. (4) Traverse input right-to-left, place each element at index C[val]-1, decrement C[val]. Complexity: O(n + k) where k = range of input. Stable: Yes. In-place: No (needs auxiliary arrays). Best when k = O(n).

Radix Sort Method Idea: Sort numbers digit by digit, starting from the least significant digit (LSD) to the most significant, using a stable sort (usually Counting Sort) at each level. Steps: Find max number of digits d. For each digit position (1s, 10s, 100s…): apply Counting Sort based on that digit only. Complexity: O(d × (n + b)) where d = digits, b = base (usually 10). Stable: Yes. In-place: No.

Bucket Sort Method Idea: Distribute elements into buckets based on their value range, sort each bucket individually, then concatenate. Steps: (1) Create n empty buckets. (2) For each element, place it in bucket[floor(n × element)]. (3) Sort each bucket (using Insertion Sort). (4) Concatenate all buckets in order. Complexity: Best/Avg O(n + k), Worst O(n²) if all elements land in one bucket. Best for uniformly distributed floating-point data in [0, 1).

Sorting Complexity Comparison Method Algorithm Best Average Worst Stable? In-place? Bubble O(n) O(n²) O(n²) Yes Yes Selection O(n²) O(n²) O(n²) No Yes Insertion O(n) O(n²) O(n²) Yes Yes Heap O(n log n) O(n log n) O(n log n) No Yes Counting O(n+k) O(n+k) O(n+k) Yes No Radix O(dn) O(dn) O(dn) Yes No Bucket O(n+k) O(n+k) O(n²) Yes No
Unit III: Dynamic Programming & Complexity CO3

Dynamic Programming (DP) Systematically exhausts all possibilities by caching solutions to overlapping subproblems (memoization/tabulation), guaranteeing a global optimum for complex state spaces. Example: Matrix Chain Multiplication optimally parenthesizes a chain of matrices in O(n^3) using a cost table.

Bellman-Ford vs Dijkstra graph LR A((S)) -- 5 --> B((U)) A -- 4 --> C((V)) B -- -6 --> C Dijkstra uses a priority queue (Greedy) but fails catastrophically with negative weights. Bellman-Ford repeatedly relaxes all edges (DP) and detects negative cycles on the V-th pass. Example: Routing in networks where path costs can become negative due to subsidies requires Bellman-Ford.

0/1 vs Fractional Knapsack Fractional allows splitting items (solvable greedily by sorting value/weight ratio). 0/1 strictly forbids splitting, invalidating the greedy choice and mandating DP. Example: Packing discrete gold bars (0/1 DP) vs packing gold dust (Fractional Greedy). Exam Trap: Applying greedy value/weight ratio to 0/1 Knapsack is the most common student error. Always use the DP table: `dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], val[i] + dp[i-1][w-wt[i]])`.

Master Method for Recurrences Method For recurrences of the form T(n) = aT(n/b) + Θ(n k ) , compute log b a and compare with k : Condition Result log b a > k T(n) = Θ(n log b a ) log b a = k T(n) = Θ(n k log n) log b a < k T(n) = Θ(n k ) Example: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n → a=2, b=2, k=1. log₂2 = 1 = k → Case 2 → T(n) = Θ(n log n). Example: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n → log₂4 = 2 > 1 → Case 1 → T(n) = Θ(n²).

Substitution Method for Recurrences Method Step 1: Guess the form of the solution (e.g., T(n) = O(n log n)). Step 2: Assume it holds for smaller values: T(n/2) ≤ c(n/2)log(n/2). Step 3: Substitute into the recurrence and prove T(n) ≤ cn log n by induction. Step 4: Verify the base case.

Binary Search Method Prerequisite: Array must be sorted. Steps: Set low=0, high=n-1. While low ≤ high: compute mid = (low+high)/2. If arr[mid] == target → found. If arr[mid] < target → search right half (low = mid+1). If arr[mid] > target → search left half (high = mid-1). Complexity: O(log n). Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1).

Merge Sort Method Idea: Divide the array into two halves, recursively sort each half, then merge them in sorted order. Steps: (1) Find mid = (low+high)/2. (2) MergeSort(low, mid) and MergeSort(mid+1, high). (3) Merge: use two pointers to compare elements from both halves, placing the smaller one into a temp array. Copy back. Complexity: Best/Worst/Avg O(n log n). Stable: Yes. In-place: No (needs O(n) auxiliary). Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).

Quick Sort Method Idea: Pick a pivot, partition the array so all elements ≤ pivot are on the left and > pivot are on the right, then recurse on both halves. Partition (Lomuto): Set pivot = arr[high], i = low-1. For j = low to high-1: if arr[j] ≤ pivot, increment i, swap arr[i] and arr[j]. Finally swap arr[i+1] with pivot. Complexity: Best/Avg O(n log n), Worst O(n²) [already sorted + bad pivot]. Randomized pivot selection avoids worst case. Stable: No. In-place: Yes.

Max-Min (Divide & Conquer) Method Idea: Find both the maximum and minimum of an array using fewer comparisons than the naive 2(n-1) approach. Steps: Divide array into two halves. Recursively find (min, max) of each half. Return min = min(left_min, right_min), max = max(left_max, right_max). Comparisons: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2 → approximately 3n/2 - 2 comparisons (vs. 2n - 2 naive).
Unit IV: Advanced Graph Algorithms CO4

Minimum Spanning Trees (MST) Acutely optimizes network connectivity. Kruskal's sorts edges globally (uses Disjoint-Set/Union-Find). Prim's grows a single tree locally from a root (uses Min-Heap). Example: Kruskal's O(E log E) is ideal for sparse graphs; Prim's O(E + V log V) with Fibonacci heaps dominates dense graphs.

Network Flow (Ford-Fulkerson) Calculates the maximum flow in a flow network. It iteratively finds augmenting paths in a residual graph until none exist. Relies heavily on the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem. Example: Maximizing water flow through a plumbing network with distinct pipe capacities. Pro Tip: The Edmonds-Karp implementation uses BFS to find augmenting paths, strictly bounding execution time to O(V E^2) unlike naive DFS.

All-Pairs Shortest Path (Floyd-Warshall) A quintessential DP algorithm computing shortest paths between all vertex pairs in O(V^3) time. It incrementally allows intermediate vertices from {1...k}. Example: Generating a complete distance matrix for a GPS routing system between all major cities.
Unit V: NP-Completeness & Approximation CO5

P vs NP Classes P: Solvable in polynomial time. NP: Solutions are verifiable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic Turing machine. Example: Sorting is in P. Sudoku solving is in NP (fast to check a solved board, hard to solve).

NP-Complete Reductions A problem Y is NP-Complete if it's in NP and every NP problem polynomial-time reduces to Y. To prove a new problem Y is NPC, reduce a known NPC problem X to Y. Example: Reducing 3-SAT (known NPC) to Clique (target Y) to prove Clique is NP-Complete. Exam Trap: Reduction direction matters! To prove Y is hard, reduce the KNOWN hard problem X to Y (X -> Y). Reducing Y to X proves nothing about Y's difficulty.

Approximation Algorithms Heuristics for NP-Hard problems that guarantee a solution within a specific multiplicative factor (ρ) of the absolute optimal cost in polynomial time. Example: The 2-Approximation for Vertex Cover using a greedy maximal matching guarantees the cover is at most twice the optimal size.

Complexity Hierarchy flowchart BT P((P)) --> NP((NP)) NPC((NP-Complete)) --> NP NPC -.-> NPH((NP-Hard)) NP -.-> NPH Example: Halting Problem is NP-Hard but not NP-Complete (since it's undecidable and thus not in NP).
